sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Distributed tracing is the practice of recording a single user request's path as a tree of spans across service boundaries, so that engineers can reconstruct causality, find the slowest hop, and explain why a particular request failed — even when fifty services touched it.
A trace is a tree of spans. Each span represents a unit of work — an HTTP call, a database query, a cache lookup, a message publish — and carries a name, a start time, a duration, a set of tags, and a parent reference. The root span is the work the user-facing entry point did; the child spans are the work that entry point's dependencies did; grandchildren extend the tree downward through the call graph. Two pieces of metadata bind the tree together: the trace ID, a single random value shared by every span in the request, and the span ID plus parent span ID, which encode the tree structure. When a request crosses a process boundary — service A calls service B over HTTP — service A injects the trace context (trace ID, current span ID, sampling flags) into the request headers, service B extracts it, creates a child span, and continues the trace. This context propagation is what distinguishes distributed tracing from logs: a log says "something happened here," a trace says "here is everything that happened, in causal order, across the whole system, for this one request." The W3C Trace Context standard (the `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers) is now the universal format, supported by every major tracer and language runtime.

The motivating example is Uber's migration from a monolith to microservices, documented in their 2017 engineering blog post "OpenTelemetry at Uber." In 2014 Uber ran a Python monolith that was straightforward to debug — a single process, a single stack trace. By 2015 they had split into a thousand microservices in Go, Node, Python, and Java, and a single ride-request touched over a hundred services. When a rider tapped "Request" and saw a spinner for thirty seconds, the team had no way to know which of those hundred services was slow. Logs existed but were scattered across services with no shared identifier; metrics existed but showed aggregates, not per-request behavior. The team adopted OpenTracing (later merged into OpenTelemetry), instrumented every service with context propagation, and shipped the spans to Jaeger, the open-source UI they wrote and donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. After deployment, the mean time to localize a latency regression dropped from days (bisection across services with synthetic probes) to minutes (open the trace, find the slow span). The lesson was that microservices without tracing are observably opaque; microservices with tracing are debuggable.

The historical origin is Google's Dapper paper (2010), which formalized the trace-tree model, sampling strategy, and collection pipeline. Twitter open-sourced a Dapper clone named Zipkin in 2012; Uber wrote Jaeger in 2016; OpenTelemetry (the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus) became the CNCF standard in 2019. The architecture is consistent across these systems: instrumented libraries generate spans, an in-process tracer batches them, a background reporter ships them to a collector, the collector writes to a storage backend (Cassandra, Elasticsearch), and a UI queries the storage and renders the trace tree. The Dapper paper's contribution was the insight that tracing at Google's scale (petabytes of spans per day) is only feasible with head-based sampling — the root service decides, at request admission, whether to record the trace, and propagates the decision in the context — because recording every request would dwarf the production traffic. Modern systems add tail-based sampling, where the collector defers the sampling decision until the trace completes and can sample selectively (always keep errors, always keep slow requests, sample the rest) — at the cost of buffering the full trace in memory until it ends.

The trade-off in tracing design is observability versus overhead. Every span generates CPU to construct, memory to buffer, network to ship, and storage to persist; at Google's scale this is non-trivial even with sampling. Head-based sampling at 0.1% is cheap but loses the long tail — errors and slow requests, which are exactly what engineers want to see, are sampled at the same rate as healthy requests and become statistically invisible. Tail-based sampling keeps every error and slow request but requires the collector to buffer each trace in memory until it completes, which is expensive for traces that take minutes. The state of the art is a hybrid: head-based sampling at 1–5% for capacity planning and aggregate latency analysis, plus tail-based sampling that keeps 100% of errors and slow requests (e.g., the slowest 1%), plus a small uniform sample of healthy traces for baseline comparison. OpenTelemetry supports this hybrid through the OpenTelemetry Collector's `tail_sampling` processor, which collects all spans by trace ID, applies policy at trace completion, and exports only the kept traces. Teams that get this right pay 1–3% request overhead for tracing that captures every important request; teams that get it wrong either drown in storage costs or miss the traces they need during incidents.

The final concept is causal analysis. Once a trace is rendered as a tree, the critical-path analysis identifies the chain of spans whose durations sum to the end-to-end latency — the spans on the path from root to the deepest leaf that consumed the most wall-clock time. Critical-path analysis is what makes tracing actionable: "the request took 800ms because the database query on the order service took 600ms, of which 580ms was spent waiting on a row lock." Without the trace, the engineer sees only "checkout is slow" and has no way to know which of fifty services to look at. With the trace, the engineer sees the exact span to investigate. Modern tracers (Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb) support span-level tags that let engineers filter traces by user ID, feature flag, error code, or any other dimension — turning the trace store into a queryable record of per-request behavior that aggregates cannot provide.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant GW as API Gateway
    participant ORD as Order Service
    participant PAY as Payment Service
    participant DB as Database
    participant K as Kafka
    U->>GW: POST /checkout (trace-id: abc123)
    GW->>ORD: forward w/ traceparent
    ORD->>DB: SELECT order (child span)
    DB-->>ORD: rows
    ORD->>PAY: charge w/ traceparent
    PAY->>DB: INSERT payment
    DB-->>PAY: ok
    PAY-->>ORD: charged
    ORD->>K: publish OrderConfirmed
    ORD-->>GW: 200 OK
    GW-->>U: response
    Note over U,K: Single trace tree: 7 spans, 1 trace-id, parent links
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
User -> Gateway -> Order -> Payment -> DB
                          -> DB
                -> Kafka

Trace tree (trace-id: abc123):
+-- Gateway.handle (root, 12ms)
    +-- Order.create (child, 8ms)
        +-- DB.query_order (3ms)        <- SELECT rows
        +-- Payment.charge (4ms)
        |   +-- DB.insert_payment (3ms) <- INSERT row
        +-- Kafka.publish (1ms)

Critical path (sum to 12ms):
  Gateway(1) -> Order(2) -> Payment(1) -> DB.insert_payment(3) ... = longest chain

Sampling decisions:
  head-based:  root picks sampled=true at 1% rate -> drop 99% at admission
  tail-based:  collector buffers trace, keeps if error OR p99 latency -> 100% of errors kept
```

### Walkthrough
1. The user's request enters the API gateway, which generates a trace ID and root span, then injects the W3C `traceparent` header into the outbound call to the order service.
2. The order service extracts the trace context, creates a child span, and propagates the context to its own dependencies — the database, the payment service, and Kafka — each of which creates a grandchild span linked by parent ID.
3. Spans are batched in-process, shipped asynchronously to a collector, which applies tail-based sampling policy (keep all errors, keep slowest 1%, sample the rest) and exports surviving traces to storage.
4. The engineer queries the trace UI by trace ID, user ID, or service+latency filter, and the UI renders the span tree with timing waterfall.
5. Critical-path analysis highlights the chain of spans whose durations sum to end-to-end latency, pointing the engineer at the exact hop to investigate — here, the database insert on the payment service.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# distributed_tracing.py - runnable; W3C trace context propagation across services
import random, time, uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Span:
    trace_id: str           # shared across whole tree
    span_id: str            # unique per span
    parent_span_id: str     # links to parent; empty for root
    name: str
    service: str
    start_ms: float
    duration_ms: float = 0.0
    tags: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    events: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def finish(self):
        self.duration_ms = (time.time() * 1000) - self.start_ms

class Tracer:
    """Minimal tracer demonstrating W3C trace-context propagation."""
    def __init__(self, service: str, sampler_rate: float = 1.0):
        self.service = service
        self.sampler_rate = sampler_rate
        self.spans: list[Span] = []

    def _new_id(self) -> str:
        return uuid.uuid4().hex[:16]

    def start_span(self, name: str, traceparent: str | None = None) -> Span:
        if traceparent:
            # parse W3C traceparent: version-traceid-parentid-flags
            parts = traceparent.split("-")
            trace_id, parent_id, flags = parts[1], parts[2], parts[3]
            sampled = flags == "01"
        else:
            trace_id = self._new_id()
            parent_id = ""
            sampled = random.random() < self.sampler_rate
        span = Span(trace_id=trace_id, span_id=self._new_id(),
                    parent_span_id=parent_id, name=name, service=self.service,
                    start_ms=time.time() * 1000,
                    tags={"sampled": sampled})
        return span

    def inject(self, span: Span) -> str:
        """Build outbound W3C traceparent header for child service."""
        flags = "01" if span.tags.get("sampled") else "00"
        return f"00-{span.trace_id}-{span.span_id}-{flags}"

    def record(self, span: Span):
        if span.tags.get("sampled"):
            self.spans.append(span)

def call_service(tracer, name, parent_traceparent, latency_ms):
    """Simulate a downstream service call with tracing."""
    span = tracer.start_span(name, parent_traceparent)
    time.sleep(latency_ms / 1000)   # simulate work
    span.finish()
    tracer.record(span)
    return tracer.inject(span)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    gw = Tracer("gateway")
    root = gw.start_span("POST /checkout")
    time.sleep(0.001); root.finish(); gw.record(root)
    tp1 = gw.inject(root)
    # order service (would be separate process in reality)
    order = Tracer("order")
    tp2 = call_service(order, "Order.create", tp1, latency_ms=8)
    # payment service, child of order
    pay = Tracer("payment")
    call_service(pay, "Payment.charge", tp2, latency_ms=4)
    print(f"Gateway spans:  {[(s.name, s.service, round(s.duration_ms,2)) for s in gw.spans]}")
    print(f"Order spans:    {[(s.name, s.service, round(s.duration_ms,2)) for s in order.spans]}")
    print(f"Payment spans:  {[(s.name, s.service, round(s.duration_ms,2)) for s in pay.spans]}")
    print(f"Trace id shared across all 3 services: {gw.spans[0].trace_id}")
```
